power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Social, Emotional, and Behavioral Skills and Work Outcomes
table.research_questions: This study will examine whether and how SEB skills relate with work-related outcomes among employed adults. We predict that SEB skills will relate with work-related outcome variables. Specifically, we predict that Self-Management Skills will relate positively with job satisfaction, organizational commitment, work engagement, low counterproductive work behavior, and conservatism values; Social Engagement Skills will relate positively with organizational commitment, low burnout, enterprising interests, self-enhancement values, and openness to change values; Cooperation Skills will relate positively with organizational commitment, social interests, and self-transcendence values; Emotional Resilience Skills will relate positively with organizational commitment, low burnout, low counterproductive work behavior, and low turnover intentions; and Innovation Skills will relate positively with work engagement, investigative interests, artistic interests, openness to change values, and self-transcendence values.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Authors’ limited observation of the data could not influence their analysis decisions. At least some of the data that will be used for this analysis plan has been accessed and observed by the authors. However, the authors certify that they have not sufficiently observed relevant evidence to influence their analysis decisions for this analysis plan and will not do so until after this plan is registered.
table.explanation_of_foreknowledge_and_managin: Data are currently being collected. Some of the contributors have begun to code O*NET occupational codes and occupational titles from participants’ responses to survey questions about their current employment. However, they have not observed or analyzed any other data from the study.
table.study_type: Non-randomized study: Does not include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes correlational studies, observational studies, surveys, natural experiments, real-world evidence studies, regression discontinuity designs, and descriptive studies.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Indirect inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to examine a potential causal relationship, but is not designed to isolate the specific causal effect. This work may inform causal inference indirectly or advance insight toward future estimation of a causal relationship.
table.study_design_overview: Participants will complete an online survey that includes measures of SEB skills, work-related outcomes, and demographics. The survey will be administered using the Qualtrics platform, and will include the BESSI as a measure of SEB skills; a battery of work-related outcomes including measures of job satisfaction, organizational commitment, burnout, job performance, work engagement, organizational citizenship behavior, counterproductive work behavior, turnover intentions, vocational interests, and work-related values; and demographic and occupational information.
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be employed adults recruited and compensated through the Prolific research participation platform. Prolific prescreening data will be used to ensure that all participants’ current employment status is full-time employed; age is between 18 and 75 years old; current country of residence is the United States; fluent languages include English; and approval rate is 95% or higher. Quota sampling will be used with Prolific prescreening data to ensure that the sample is approximately representative of the US employed adult population in terms of age (10% ages 18-24, 25% ages 25-34, 25% ages 35-44, 20% ages 45-54, 20% ages 55-75) and sex (50% male, 50% female). Participants will be compensated $4 USD for completing the research survey.
table.sample_size: The target sample size will be at least 700 participants.
table.sample_size_rationale: The target sample size is intended to maximize statistical power and descriptive precision within the available funding for the study. The target sample size provides 80% power to detect true correlations of 0.11 or stronger, and 95% power to detect true correlations of 0.14 or stronger, at the alpha = 0.05 significance level.
table.stopping_rule: Data collection will terminate when all funds approved for participant compensation have been spent.
table.measured_variables:
SEB skills will be measured using items from the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI; Soto et al., 2022).

Employment type, industry, occupation, duties, hours, and income will be measured using items from American Community Survey (ACS; U.S. Census Bureau, 2024).

Job satisfaction will be measured using items from the Michigan Organizational Assessment Questionnaire – Job Satisfaction Subscale (MOAQ-JSS; Cammann et al., 1983).

Organizational commitment will be measured using items from the International Social Survey Programme Work Orientations Module – Affective Organizational Commitment Scale (ISSP; Urban et al., 2023).

Burnout will be measured using items from the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory (OLBI; Demerouti et al., 2001).

Job performance will be measured using items from the In-Role Behavior Scale (IRB; Williams & Anderson, 1991).

Work engagement will be measured using items from the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale – 3-Item Ultra-Short Version (UWES-3; Schaufeli et al., 2019).

Organizational citizenship behavior will be measured using items from the Organizational Citizenship Behavior Checklist (OCB-C-10; Spector et al., 2010).

Counterproductive work behavior will be measured using items from the Counterproductive Work Behavior Checklist (CWB-C-10; ; Spector et al., 2010).

Turnover intentions will be measured using items from the Michigan Organizational Assessment Questionnaire – Turnover Intention Scale (MOAQ-TI; Cammann et al., 1983).

Occupational interests will be measured using items from the O*NET Mini Interest Profiler (O*NET Mini-IP; Rounds et al., 2016).

Work values will be measured using items from the Work Values Survey (WVS; Cable & Edwards, 2004).

Demographic characteristics (age, gender, sex, ethnicity, race, education level, income) will be measured using self-report items.

See the attached file for the complete research survey.
table.indices: All multi-item measures will be scored as means of the corresponding item responses.
table.statistical_tests: To test relations between SEB skills and work outcomes, we will (a) compute zero-order correlations of the BESSI skill domains with the outcome measures, (b) compute partial correlations controlling for age and gender, (c) regress each convergent and outcome measure on the set of five BESSI skill domains, and (d) repeat these regressions with age and gender included as control variables.
table.transformations:
Occupation will be coded by human and AI coders using 8-digit codes and titles from the O*NET Standard Occupational Classification system. Disagreements will be resolved through review and discussion. All occupational coding will be finalized before conducting any analyses that relate occupation with other variables.

To normalize the distribution of income, raw income values may be transformed (e.g., using a log transformation), and outliers may be recoded (e.g., to the closest observed value within three standard deviations of the mean). These decisions may be informed by descriptive analyses of the income distribution, but all decisions regarding transformations and outliers will be finalized before conducting any analyses that relate income with other variables.
table.inference_criteria: We will conduct all hypothesis tests at the alpha = .05 significance level (two-tailed). To account for testing multiple hypotheses, interpretation of results will focus on (a) tests of the pre-registered hypotheses, and (b) results that are robust across analytic approaches (e.g., correlation vs. regression analyses, and analyses that include vs. exclude demographic control variables).
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Participants will be fully excluded from analysis if they complete the survey in less than one third of the median completion time, or fail the attention-check and bot screener items embedded in the survey. Within each measure, participants will be coded as missing if they answer fewer than 50% of the items for that measure.
table.missing_data_handling: After applying the data exclusion criteria, all remaining missing item responses will be replaced with the mean response for that item rounded to the nearest possible response value.

text.text: Personality traits are long-established correlates of occupational success.
Recently, researchers have also begun to examine the role of social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills in key life domains.
Conceptualized as functional capacities rather than characteristic tendencies, SEB skills represent what individuals are capable of doing when wanted or needed.
The present research examined how the five major skill domains assessed by the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI) relate with consequential work criteria and outcomes.

Specifically, using a demographically representative sample of 1,064 working adults, we tested preregistered links of SEB skills with work performance, attainment, attitudes, intentions, behaviors, interests, and values.
SEB skills related robustly with these criteria and outcomes, with different skill domains showing distinctive relationships.

For example, Self-Management Skills were linked with self-perceived performance; Social Engagement Skills with occupational attainment; Cooperation Skills with prosocial interests and values; Emotional Resilience Skills with positive work attitudes; and Innovation Skills with creative interests and values.
Short forms of the BESSI retained considerable predictive power, making them highly suitable for applied contexts.

These findings highlight the key role of functional capacities in occupational experiences and provide a foundation for integrating SEB skills into personnel selection, career coaching, and organizational research.
People's career trajectories, from the jobs they select to their performance and ultimate success, are shaped by many factors.
Beyond technical knowledge, these factors also include interpersonal and self-regulatory capabilities.

These latter characteristics, sometimes colloquially termed "soft skills," are increasingly recognized as important determinants of life success, because they relate with criteria and outcomes ranging from academic achievement and vocational interests to workplace attitudes and performance (Heckman & Kautz, 2012).
text.formatted: These latter characteristics, sometimes colloquially termed "soft skills," are increasingly recognized as important determinants of life success, because they relate with criteria and outcomes ranging from academic achievement and vocational interests to workplace attitudes and performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Heckman & Kautz, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: To bring conceptual clarity to this domain, researchers have recently organized these capabilities under the framework of social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills.
Specifically, SEB skills are defined as a person's capacities to maintain social relationships, regulate emotions, manage goaldirected behaviors, and learn from novel experiences (Soto et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Specifically, SEB skills are defined as a person's capacities to maintain social relationships, regulate emotions, manage goaldirected behaviors, and learn from novel experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Soto et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: By focusing on functional capacities, SEB skills capture what individuals are capable of doing, beyond what they typically do.

Understanding these skills is important for both organizational science and applied practice, because they provide a framework for conceptualizing and assessing the capabilities that individuals need to succeed in their careers.
Despite the growing recognition of SEB skills, empirical research investigating their specific implications for the workplace is still emerging.

While a robust literature demonstrates that general personality traits relate with occupational success, researchers have only recently begun to systematically examine the distinctive role of SEB skills (Chen et al., 2024; Soto et al., 2022 Soto et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: While a robust literature demonstrates that general personality traits relate with occupational success, researchers have only recently begun to systematically examine the distinctive role of SEB skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Soto et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Soto et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the present research addresses two fundamental questions.
First, do the major domains of SEB skills relate with a broad array of consequential work criteria and outcomes?

To answer this question, we examine how SEB skills relate with an extensive set of indicators, including occupational performance and attainment, work attitudes, workplace intentions and behaviors, vocational interests, and work values.
Second, are these skill-outcome links retained when assessing skills with brief measurement tools?

To address this, we explore whether the specific links and overall predictive power of SEB skills are retained when using short-form assessments, which are often preferred in applied organizational contexts.
Social, emotional, and behavioral skills represent the functional capabilities that enable individuals to navigate interpersonal, intrapersonal, and task-directed challenges.

Historically, researchers and practitioners have proposed a dizzying array of frameworks for 21st century competencies, noncognitive skills, soft skills, durable skills, and related constructs (Berg et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Historically, researchers and practitioners have proposed a dizzying array of frameworks for 21st century competencies, noncognitive skills, soft skills, durable skills, and related constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Berg et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, recent taxonomic work (Abrahams et al., 2019; Casillas et al., 2023; OECD, 2015; Soto et al., 2021 Soto et al., , 2022;; Walton et al., 2021) has consistently found that many specific SEB skills can be organized in terms of five major domains: Self-Management Skills (used to effectively pursue goals and complete tasks), Social Engagement Skills (used to actively engage with other people), Cooperation Skills (used to maintain positive social relationships), Emotional Resilience Skills (used to regulate emotions and moods), and Innovation Skills (used to engage with novel ideas and experiences).
text.formatted: However, recent taxonomic work <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abrahams et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Casillas et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">OECD, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Soto et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Soto et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Walton et al., 2021)</ref> has consistently found that many specific SEB skills can be organized in terms of five major domains: Self-Management Skills (used to effectively pursue goals and complete tasks), Social Engagement Skills (used to actively engage with other people), Cooperation Skills (used to maintain positive social relationships), Emotional Resilience Skills (used to regulate emotions and moods), and Innovation Skills (used to engage with novel ideas and experiences).

text.text: Notably, these five SEB skill domains closely resemble the widely studied Big Five personality traits in terms of their behavioral referents (John et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Notably, these five SEB skill domains closely resemble the widely studied Big Five personality traits in terms of their behavioral referents <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(John et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Both Self-Management Skills and trait Conscientiousness center on task-and goal-related behaviors; Social Engagement Skills and trait Extraversion on agentic social behaviors; Cooperation Skills and trait Agreeableness on prosocial behaviors; Emotional Resilience Skills and trait Emotional Stability on behaviors to regulate negative affect; and Innovation Skills and Openness to Experience on cognitive and behavioral responses to novelty.

It is therefore unsurprising that traits and skills relate substantially with each other, while still remaining conceptually and empirically distinguishable (Ringwald et al., 2026; Soto et al., 2022 Soto et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: It is therefore unsurprising that traits and skills relate substantially with each other, while still remaining conceptually and empirically distinguishable <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Ringwald et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Soto et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Soto et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, traits describe behavioral tendencies (how someone tends to behave, averaged across different kinds of situations), whereas skills more directly capture behavioral capacities (how someone is capable of behaving when they want or need to do so in a particular situation).

For instance, an employee may tend to be disorganized in their personal life (low trait Conscientiousness), but also be quite capable of managing their goals, tasks, and time while completing important work projects (high Self-Management Skills).

From an organizational science perspective, the difference between functional capacities and behavioral tendencies resembles the established distinction between maximum and typical job performance (Sackett et al., 1988).
text.formatted: From an organizational science perspective, the difference between functional capacities and behavioral tendencies resembles the established distinction between maximum and typical job performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Sackett et al., 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas typical performance reflects a worker's baseline, day-to-day output, maximum performance captures what that worker can achieve when they are deliberately maximizing their effort.
Thus, personality traits are akin to typical performance, whereas SEB skills are analogous to maximum performance.

Maximum workplace performance has distinctive correlates (Beus & Whitman, 2012; Klehe & Anderson, 2007; Marcus et al., 2007; Turner, 1978), suggesting that SEB skills may also be linked with consequential work criteria and outcomes.
text.formatted: Maximum workplace performance has distinctive correlates <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Beus & Whitman, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Klehe & Anderson, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Marcus et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Turner, 1978)</ref>, suggesting that SEB skills may also be linked with consequential work criteria and outcomes.

text.text: Because SEB skills are defined as functional capacities, they should be measured using methods that align with this conceptualization.

Traditional personality inventories ask respondents to rate how accurately a series of adjectives or statements describe their typical behavior, thereby capturing characteristic tendencies (i.e., traits).
However, measuring functional capacities requires assessing how well an individual can perform specific behaviors, rather than how often they typically enact them (Soto et al., 2021).
text.formatted: However, measuring functional capacities requires assessing how well an individual can perform specific behaviors, rather than how often they typically enact them <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Soto et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI; Soto et al., 2022) was developed to address this need.
text.formatted: The Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Soto et al., 2022)</ref> was developed to address this need.

text.text: The BESSI explicitly prompts respondents to rate their proficiency across a series of 192 specific behaviors.
These ratings are then aggregated into scores indexing the five major SEB skill domains.

The BESSI has demonstrated considerable reliability and validity in previous studies using student, community, and online samples (Napolitano et al., 2025; Ringwald et al., 2026; Sewell et al., 2025; Soto et al., 2022 Soto et al., , 2023 Soto et al., , 2024;; Yoon et al., 2024), and was therefore selected to assess SEB skills in the present research.
text.formatted: The BESSI has demonstrated considerable reliability and validity in previous studies using student, community, and online samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Napolitano et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Ringwald et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Sewell et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Soto et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Soto et al., , 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Soto et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Yoon et al., 2024)</ref>, and was therefore selected to assess SEB skills in the present research.

text.text: An extensive research literature spanning industrial-organizational and personality psychology has established robust links of personality traits with a broad range of workplace criteria and outcomes.

Although there is now emerging interest in the organizational implications of SEB skills, researchers have only recently begun to examine these relationships using the taxonomic framework defined and assessed by the BESSI.
Therefore, the primary goal of the present research is to examine how SEB skills relate with a broad range of consequential work criteria and outcomes.

Because the major SEB skill domains parallel the Big Five traits in terms of their behavioral referents, the established trait literature provides a strong foundation for predicting how these skills will function in occupational contexts.

Specifically, meta-analyses examining personality traits in the workplace, as well as recent studies using the BESSI (Chen et al., 2024; Soto et al., 2022 Soto et al., , 2024)), can be used to derive hypotheses regarding the expected links of SEB skills with consequential work criteria and outcomes, while also acknowledging that the conceptual and empirical distinction between traits as behavioral tendencies and skills as functional capacities introduces some uncertainty concerning these predictions.

text.text: Regarding occupational attainment and job performance, extensive meta-analytic research demonstrates that personality traits are meaningful correlates of both objective career success and day-to-day productivity.

For example, trait Conscientiousness and Extraversion often show modest positive associations with higher earnings, occupational prestige, and promotional advancement (Alderotti et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2005; Vella, 2024).
text.formatted: For example, trait Conscientiousness and Extraversion often show modest positive associations with higher earnings, occupational prestige, and promotional advancement <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alderotti et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Ng et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Vella, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, trait Conscientiousness is recognized as a general correlate of job performance across occupations, while Extraversion relates with performance in specific roles, such as management and teamwork-intensive positions (Barrick et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Similarly, trait Conscientiousness is recognized as a general correlate of job performance across occupations, while Extraversion relates with performance in specific roles, such as management and teamwork-intensive positions <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barrick et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Because SEB skills represent the functional capacities that individuals deploy to navigate workplace demands, multiple skill domains may relate with these outcomes.

We therefore investigate whether Self-Management Skills, which encompass capacities for goal and task regulation, and Social Engagement Skills, which include capacities for group leadership and persuasive communication, are the most relevant skill correlates of occupational attainment and self-perceived job performance.
Turning to work attitudes, foundational meta-analytic reviews demonstrate that personality traits relate with how employees experience and evaluate their work environments.
Low trait Emotional Stability serves as a vulnerability factor that predisposes individuals to job burnout, whereas Extraversion protects against this negative outcome (Swider & Zimmerman, 2010).
text.formatted: Low trait Emotional Stability serves as a vulnerability factor that predisposes individuals to job burnout, whereas Extraversion protects against this negative outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Swider & Zimmerman, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Trait Conscientiousness, as well as the corresponding skill domain of Self-Management, consistently relate with job satisfaction (Chen et al., 2024; Judge et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Trait Conscientiousness, as well as the corresponding skill domain of Self-Management, consistently relate with job satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Judge et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Both Conscientiousness and Openness to Experience show distinctive relationships with work engagement (Fukuzaki & Iwata, 2022), whereas all of the Big Five traits other than Openness are moderately linked with organizational commitment (Choi et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Both Conscientiousness and Openness to Experience show distinctive relationships with work engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fukuzaki & Iwata, 2022)</ref>, whereas all of the Big Five traits other than Openness are moderately linked with organizational commitment <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Choi et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that specific SEB skill domains should provide the functional capacities needed to navigate workplace stressors and build rewarding occupational experiences.

We therefore hypothesize that (a) Self-Management Skills will positively relate with job satisfaction, because the capacity to systematically execute work tasks should facilitate the attainment and enjoyment of workplace rewards; (b) Self-Management and Innovation Skills will positively relate with work engagement, because these capacities enable workers to maintain disciplined effort and adapt proactively to job demands; (c) Emotional Resilience and Social Engagement Skills will negatively relate with burnout, because emotional resilience protects against the exhaustion associated with chronic stress, while social engagement prevents psychological distancing and depersonalization; and (d) multiple skill domains (Self-Management, Social Engagement, Cooperation, and Emotional Resilience) will positively relate with organizational commitment, reflecting the varied pathways (such as achievement, relationship-building, and effectively coping with challenges) through which employees build strong psychological attachments to their organizations.
Regarding work behaviors and intentions, previous meta-analytic research has summarized how personality traits relate with employees' discretionary actions and turnover intentions.
For example, the tendency to engage in positive organizational citizenship behavior relates modestly with multiple trait domains (Chiaburu et al., 2011).
text.formatted: For example, the tendency to engage in positive organizational citizenship behavior relates modestly with multiple trait domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chiaburu et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, counterproductive work behavior represents actions that harm the organization or its members, and relates distinctively with low Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability, as well as the corresponding skill domains of low Self-Management and Emotional Resilience (Berry et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Conversely, counterproductive work behavior represents actions that harm the organization or its members, and relates distinctively with low Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability, as well as the corresponding skill domains of low Self-Management and Emotional Resilience <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Berry et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Chen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, for the cognitive process of withdrawal, specifically turnover intentions, low Emotional Stability serves as the primary trait correlate of intentions to quit (Zimmerman, 2008).
text.formatted: Similarly, for the cognitive process of withdrawal, specifically turnover intentions, low Emotional Stability serves as the primary trait correlate of intentions to quit <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Zimmerman, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The parallels between behavioral tendencies and functional capacities suggest that key SEB skills should relate with how well employees navigate opportunities and challenges in the workplace.

We specifically hypothesize that Self-Management and Emotional Resilience Skills will relate negatively with counterproductive work behavior, because the capacities to regulate impulses and manage negative emotions can help prevent harmful actions in response to workplace stressors.

Moreover, we hypothesize that Emotional Resilience Skills will relate negatively with turnover intentions, because the capacity to cope with work-related stress protects employees against the emotional exhaustion that typically precipitates the desire to leave an organization.

Finally, because citizenship encompasses a wide array of prosocial and proactive behaviors, we explore whether multiple SEB skill domains show modest, positive relations with organizational citizenship behavior.
As for vocational interests, meta-analytic work has mapped meaningful connections between personality traits and preferences for particular occupational environments.
Most notably, this work aligns the Big Five traits with Holland's typology of realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising, and conventional interests (Barrick et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Most notably, this work aligns the Big Five traits with Holland's typology of realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising, and conventional interests <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barrick et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: For example, trait Openness to Experience is linked with investigative and artistic interests, reflecting a shared emphasis on intellectual curiosity and creativity.

Moreover, trait Extraversion relates with enterprising interests, whereas Agreeableness relates with social interests, demonstrating that energetic and cooperative dispositions fit with work environments requiring persuasion and interpersonal support, respectively.
Indeed, recent research with student samples has found links between these interests and the corresponding SEB skills domains (Soto et al., 2022 (Soto et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: Indeed, recent research with student samples has found links between these interests and the corresponding SEB skills domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Soto et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Soto et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: We therefore expect that specific SEB skill domains will align with vocational interests among working adults.

Specifically, we hypothesize that (a) Innovation Skills will relate positively with investigative and artistic interests, reflecting the capacity to engage with novel ideas and complex abstraction; (b) Cooperation Skills will relate positively with social interests, because the capacity to maintain positive relationships is important for roles focused on helping and collaborating; and (c) Social Engagement Skills will relate positively with enterprising interests, given that the capacity to actively lead and persuade others is a key asset in competitive business environments.
Regarding work values, the extant literature shows that personality traits are systematically linked with the personal values that individuals are most motivated to pursue.
Drawing on Schwartz's universal values framework (Schwartz, 1992), this research indicates that the Big Five traits map predictably onto broad motivational dimensions.
text.formatted: Drawing on Schwartz's universal values framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Schwartz, 1992)</ref>, this research indicates that the Big Five traits map predictably onto broad motivational dimensions.

text.text: For example, selfenhancement values align with trait Extraversion, conservation values with Conscientiousness, Self-Transcendence values with both Agreeableness and Openness to Experience, and openness to change values with trait Openness and Extraversion (Parks-Leduc et al., 2015).

text.text: Beyond the conceptual hypotheses regarding links of SEB skills with work criteria and outcomes derived above, there is also the practical question of how to measure SEB skills in applied settings.

Although comprehensive skill inventories like the BESSI can robustly assess individuals' functional capacities, the demands of industrial-organizational research and realworld organizational practice often dictate a need for brevity.

In applied contexts, such as largescale employee surveys, selection batteries, and talent development programs, practitioners often face constraints regarding administration time and respondent attention.
Lengthy assessments require employees to take time away from their primary work tasks, and can also induce survey fatigue that compromises data quality and reduces completion rates.
Thus, in applied settings, brief assessments may capture essential skill domains without imposing undue burdens on workers (e.g., Stanton et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Thus, in applied settings, brief assessments may capture essential skill domains without imposing undue burdens on workers (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Stanton et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: However, such measures necessarily sacrifice some reliability and validity for gains in efficiency, and these tradeoffs are most pronounced for extremely brief assessments (Credé et al., 2012; Soto & John, 2019).
text.formatted: However, such measures necessarily sacrifice some reliability and validity for gains in efficiency, and these tradeoffs are most pronounced for extremely brief assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Credé et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Soto & John, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: To meet the need for efficient assessment of SEB skills, Sewell and colleagues (2025) recently developed and validated three short forms of the BESSI.
text.formatted: To meet the need for efficient assessment of SEB skills, <ref type="bibr">Sewell and colleagues (2025)</ref> recently developed and validated three short forms of the BESSI.

text.text: Although the original, 192item BESSI is a comprehensive measure of functional capacities, its length can preclude use in time-restricted research and applied contexts.
Therefore, Sewell and colleagues (2025) used conceptual and empirical criteria to construct 96-item, 45-item, and 20-item versions of the inventory.
The BESSI-96 reduces administration time to approximately eight minutes, while the BESSI-45 and BESSI-20 require only about four minutes and two minutes to complete, respectively.

Importantly, analyses of multiple independent samples across two languages and cultural contexts indicated that these short forms retain the five-domain structure and strong reliability of the full inventory.
Moreover, they preserve the vast majority of the original measure's predictive power, ensuring that researchers and practitioners can efficiently assess individuals' SEB skills.

Building on the initial validity evidence for these short forms, it remains important to determine whether their robust psychometric characteristics extend to relations with consequential work criteria and outcomes.
Therefore, a secondary goal of the present research is to explore whether links of SEB skills with work criteria and outcomes are retained when using the BESSI short forms.

By systematically comparing the overall predictive power and the pattern of skill-outcome associations across the full-length inventory and its abbreviated versions, we aim to provide guidance for researchers and practitioners who wish to use efficient measurement tools in applied workplace settings.
In sum, previous research has established robust links between behavioral tendencies, traditionally assessed as personality traits, and a wide array of workplace criteria and outcomes.
Moreover, recent taxonomic work has brought conceptual clarity to the literature on functional capacities by organizing social, emotional, and behavioral skills into five major domains.
However, empirical research systematically investigating the specific implications of these capacities for the workplace is still emerging.

Participants were 1,064 full-time working adults in the United States.

Quota sampling was used to ensure that the sample was approximately representative of the working adult population in terms of age (9.4% ages 18-24, 25.8% ages 25-34, 24.8% ages 35-44, 20.2% ages 45-54, 19.8% ages 55 to 73, M = 41.43, SD = 12.77), and balanced in terms of sex (50.1% male, 49.9% female).

Regarding gender identity, 49.4% of participants identified as men, 49.1% as women, and 1.2% as non-binary, with 0.3% preferring not to say. 1 As for race and ethnicity, 75.8% identified as White, 16.7% as Black or African-American, 7.3% as Asian or Asian-American, 7.2% as Hispanic, Latino, or Spanish origin, 2.0% as American Indian or Alaska Native, 0.3% as Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and 2.3% as some other identity, with 10.3% of participants endorsing more than one racial or ethnic identity.

text.text: Regarding education, 0.8% did not hold any diploma or degree, 10.8% held a high school diploma, 13.8% had some college credit but no degree, 51.2% held an associate's or bachelor's degree, and 23.3% held a master's degree or higher.
All participants were recruited through the Prolific research participation platform, then provided informed consent and completed the research survey through Qualtrics.

The survey included measures of demographic characteristics, SEB skills, current occupation, self-perceived performance, job satisfaction, organizational commitment, burnout, organizational citizenship behavior, counterproductive work behavior, turnover intentions, vocational interests, and work values.
These measures were divided into two blocks, with their order counterbalanced across participants.
The median completion time was approximately 24 minutes, and participants were compensated at least $4 USD via Prolific.
This research was performed in line with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and was approved by the [blinded for review] Institutional Review Board (Protocol #2026-1).
Self-Management, Social Engagement, Cooperation, Emotional Resilience, and Innovation Skills were assessed using the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI; Soto et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Self-Management, Social Engagement, Cooperation, Emotional Resilience, and Innovation Skills were assessed using the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Soto et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This measure's 192 items are brief descriptions of behavior (e.g., "lead a group of people," "show up for things on time," "stay calm in stressful situations").
Participants rated how well they could perform each behavior on a five-point competence scale ranging from1 = not at all well to5 = extremely well.

To compare skill-outcome relations and overall predictive power across longer and shorter versions of the BESSI, we scored the five major skill domains from the full-length inventory, as well as from the item subsets included in its 96-item, 45-item, and 20-item short forms (BESSI-96, BESSI-45, and BESSI-20; Sewell et al., 2025).

text.text: In the present sample, McDonald's omega reliabilities on the full-length BESSI were .98 for Self-Management, .95 for Social Engagement, .94 for Cooperation, .97 for Emotional Resilience, and .94 for Innovation Skills.
Omega reliabilities ranged from .90 to .95 for the BESSI-96, from .81 to .92 for the BESSI-45, and from .68 to .83 for the BESSI-20.

Participants responded to questions from the American Community Survey (U.S. Census Bureau, 2024) to assess their current type of employment (e.g., private-sector employee, government employee, self-employed), kind of business or industry, main occupation, and most important activities or duties.
They then responded to questions assessing their managerial level, number of hours worked per week, and income earned from this job.
Managerial level was coded as1 = do not supervise employees,2 = supervise employees who are not managers or supervisors,3 = supervise other managers or supervisors.
Earnings were scaled to dollars per year and then natural log-transformed to reduce positive skew.

Occupation and occupational attainment were coded using the O*NET Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) system, based on responses to the survey questions assessing type of employment, kind of business or industry, main occupation, most important activities or duties, and managerial level.
Coding was independently performed by a human researcher (the second author) and an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (Google Gemini 3.1 Pro).
Discrepancies were then resolved through review and discussion by the first and second authors.

There was exact agreement between the human and AI coders in 75.5% of cases (κ = .74) at the SOC twodigit (major group) level, 65.9% of cases (κ = .66) at the three-digit (minor group) level, 60.8% of cases (κ = .61) at the five-digit (broad occupation) level, and 56.1% of cases (κ = .56) at the eight-digit (detailed occupation) level.
Regarding discrepancies, 55.2% were resolved by adopting the human-suggested code and 44.8% by adopting the AI-suggested code.

These agreement rates are very similar to those observed between expert human coders, suggesting that AI tools can supplement but not necessarily replace human coding expertise (Putka et al., 2023; Russ et al., 2016).

text.text: After finalizing the eight-digit occupation codes, the O*NET job zone for each occupation was recorded as an index of occupational attainment.

Job zones represent groups of occupations that are similar in terms of the amount of education, related experience, and on-the job training needed to successfully perform the work (2 = very little to some preparation,3 = medium preparation,4 = considerable preparation,5 = extensive preparation).
Self-perceived job performance was assessed using the In-Role Behavior scale (Williams & Anderson, 1991).

text.text: These results indicate that older adults tended to score slightly higher on Self-Management, Social Engagement, and Emotional Resilience skills, whereas younger adults scored higher on Innovation Skills.
Regarding gender, women tended to score slightly higher on Cooperation Skills, whereas men scored higher on Emotional Resilience Skills.
However, all of these correlations were small in size (absolute r ≤ 0.10), indicating relatively modest demographic differences in SEB skills.
Our primary, preregistered analyses tested links of SEB skill domains with consequential work criteria and outcomes.

Specifically, we (a) computed zero-order correlations of skills with criteria and outcomes, (b) computed partial correlations controlling for age and gender, (c) regressed each criteria or outcome on the set of five skill domains (to control for overlap between the skill domains themselves), and (d) regressed each criteria or outcome on the five skill domains, age, and gender.

The partial correlations and regression coefficients controlling for age and gender are presented in Table 3; additional results, including zero-order correlations, regression coefficients without demographic controls, and confidence intervals, are presented in Supplemental Table S2.

text.text: We therefore focus our interpretation on these highly robust skill-outcome links.

Regarding occupational attainment and self-perceived performance, Social Engagement Skills related consistently with occupational attainment (β = .19 when controlling for gender, age, and the other four skill domains), managerial level (β = .43), and earnings (β = .20), while Self-Management Skills related robustly with perceived performance (β = .52).

As for work attitudes, Emotional Resilience Skills related consistently with job satisfaction (β = .28), organizational commitment (β = .20), work engagement (β = .22), and low burnout (β = -.41); work engagement was also linked with Social Engagement Skills (β = .24).
Concerning work behaviors and intentions, organizational citizenship behavior related with the combination of Social Engagement (β = .31), Cooperation (β = .22), and Innovation Skills (β = .15).
Self-Management Skills related with low counterproductive work behavior (β = -.27) and turnover intentions (β = -.19); the latter was also linked with Emotional Resilience Skills (β = -.16).

As for vocational interests, Innovation Skills related robustly with both artistic (β = .75) and investigative (β = .36) interests, Social Engagement Skills related with enterprising interests (β = .50), and Emotional Resilience Skills related with conventional interests (β = .23).

Social interests related with the combination of Cooperation (β = .44), Social Engagement (β = .20), and Innovation Skills (β = .16), whereas realistic interests related with Emotional Resilience (β = .25) and Innovation Skills (β = .19).

Regarding work values, Cooperation Skills related robustly with the self-transcendence values of relationships with others (β = .53) and altruism (β = .50); the former was also linked with Social Engagement Skills (β = .27), whereas the latter was linked with Innovation Skills (β = .19).
Social Engagement Skills related consistently with the self-enhancement values of prestige (β = .47) and pay (β = .23); the latter was also linked with Self-Management Skills (β = .24).

Self-Management Skills related consistently with the conservation values of security (β = .41) and authority (β = .19); the former was also linked with Cooperation Skills (β = .20), whereas the latter was linked with Social Engagement Skills (β = .36).

Finally, Innovation Skills related consistently with the openness to change values of variety (β = .32) and autonomy (β = .22); the former was also linked with Social Engagement (β = .19) and Cooperation (β = .15) Skills, whereas the latter was linked with Self-Management Skills (β = .19).

Beyond these primary analyses, we also conducted exploratory analyses investigating the extent to which the BESSI short forms (BESSI-96, BESSI-45, and BESSI-20) reproduced the skill-outcome links and overall predictive power demonstrated by the full-length BESSI skill domains.

To do this, we repeated the four sets of analyses described above (zero-order correlations, partial correlations controlling for age and gender, and regressions with and without demographic controls) for each of the BESSI short forms.

We then computed vector correlations (i.e., the correlation between the set of five coefficients for the full-length BESSI domains vs. a set of five short-form domains) to index the consistency of skill-outcome associations, and computed explained-variance ratios (i.e., R² when predicting a work criterion or outcome from a BESSI short form divided by R² when predicting from the full-length BESSI) to index the BESSI short forms' predictive power relative to the full-length measure.
The similarity vector correlations and explained-variance ratios from these analyses are presented in Table 4, and additional results are presented in Supplemental Tables S3 to S5.

text.text: Regarding consistency in the pattern of skill-outcome associations, when averaged across the 25 work criteria and outcomes, vector correlations comparing the set of five skill domain coefficients between the full-length BESSI and BESSI-96 averaged greater than .99 when comparing the zero-order correlations, regressions without demographic controls, and regressions with demographic controls; they averaged .98 when comparing the partial correlations controlling for age and gender.
For the BESSI-45, the vector correlations averaged .98 when comparing the zero-order or partial correlations, and averaged .99 when comparing the regressions with or without demographic controls.

Finally, for the BESSI-20, the vector correlations averaged .97 when comparing the zero-order correlations, .94 when comparing the partial correlations, and .96 when comparing the regressions with or without demographic controls.

Of the 40 skill-outcome links that were highly significant (p < .001) across all four sets of analyses for the full-length BESSI, 38 remained highly significant across all analyses for the BESSI-96, all 40 were highly significant for the BESSI-45, and 37 were highly significant for the BESSI-20.

text.text: As for the overall predictive power of the short forms, when averaged across work criteria and outcomes, the BESSI-96 skill domains retained approximately 97% of the full-length BESSI's predictive power when excluding demographic controls, or 98% after including such controls.
The BESSI-45 skill domains retained approximately 94%, and the BESSI-20 about 85%, of the full-length measure's predictive power, regardless of whether demographic controls were included or excluded.
Taken together, these results indicate that the pattern of links of SEB skill domains with work criteria and outcomes is very similar between the full-length BESSI and its short forms.

Moreover, they show that the BESSI-96 and BESSI-45 skill domains retain almost all of the full-length measure's predictive power, whereas the BESSI-20 shows a more substantial reduction in predictive power.
The present findings support two key conclusions.
First, SEB skills relate robustly with a broad range of consequential work criteria and outcomes, with different skill domains showing distinctive relationships with different criteria and outcomes.

Even when evaluated against a strict standard of evidence (p < .001 across four sets of analyses), Self-Management Skills related consistently with self-perceived job performance, low counterproductive work behavior and turnover intentions, and valuing pay, security, authority, and autonomy.
text.formatted: Even when evaluated against a strict standard of evidence (p < .001 across four sets of analyses), Self-Management Skills related consistently with self-perceived job performance, low counterproductive work behavior and turnover intentions, and valuing pay, security, authority, and autonomy.

text.text: Social Engagement Skills related consistently with occupational attainment, managerial level, earnings, work engagement, organizational citizenship behavior, social and enterprising interests, and valuing relationships with others, pay, prestige, authority and variety.
Cooperation Skills related consistently with organizational citizenship behavior, social interests, and valuing altruism, relationships with others, security, and variety.
Emotional Resilience Skills related consistently with job satisfaction, organizational commitment, work engagement, low burnout and turnover intentions, and realistic and conventional interests.
Finally, Innovation Skills related consistently with organizational citizenship behavior, realistic, investigative, artistic, and social interests, and valuing altruism, variety, and autonomy.

Notably, every one of the 25 consequential work criteria and outcomes examined here was consistently linked with at least one SEB skill domain, and each skill domain related with a distinctive set of criteria and outcomes.

These findings highlight the importance of social, emotional, and behavioral skills for understanding the occupations that people choose to pursue, their reasons for doing so, and their performance, attainment, attitudes, intentions, and behaviors once on the job.

A second key conclusion is that when predicting work criteria and outcomes from the five major SEB skill domains, the BESSI-96 and BESSI-45 short forms preserve almost all of the full-length BESSI's predictive power, as well as the distinctive patterns of skill-outcome relations.
The BESSI-20 also preserves the general pattern of skill-outcome relations, but with a more substantial reduction in overall predictive power.
These findings have important implications for both researchers and practitioners interested in SEB skills and occupational success.

For example, by linking social, emotional, and behavioral skills with work performance, attainment, attitudes, intentions, behaviors, interests, and values, the present findings further extend the nomological network of SEB skills into the workplace (Chen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, by linking social, emotional, and behavioral skills with work performance, attainment, attitudes, intentions, behaviors, interests, and values, the present findings further extend the nomological network of SEB skills into the workplace <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas previous studies of SEB skills have predominantly focused on adolescent and young adult student populations (Napolitano et al., 2025; Soto et al., 2023 Soto et al., , 2024;; Yoon et al., 2024), the present research examines such skills among working adults.
text.formatted: Whereas previous studies of SEB skills have predominantly focused on adolescent and young adult student populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Napolitano et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Soto et al., 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Soto et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Yoon et al., 2024)</ref>, the present research examines such skills among working adults.

text.text: It therefore advances our knowledge regarding the lifelong importance of SEB skills across life domains and developmental periods.

Moreover, establishing the relevance of these capabilities for working adults also highlights a need for future research to investigate whether and how SEB skills relate to functioning in other adult contexts, such as family dynamics, community involvement, health, and quality of life.
A second key implication concerns personnel selection and assessment.
Traditionally, research and practice in this domain have focused on personality traits as correlates of occupational success (Barrick et al., 2001; Judge et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Traditionally, research and practice in this domain have focused on personality traits as correlates of occupational success <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barrick et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Judge et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: However, the present findings indicate that SEB skills also relate with a wide array of consequential work criteria and outcomes.

This aligns with previous scholarship in industrial-organizational psychology that has examined the correlates of maximum performance, which is analogous to SEB skills as behavioral capacities (Beus & Whitman, 2012; Klehe & Anderson, 2007; Marcus et al., 2007; Sackett et al., 1988).
text.formatted: This aligns with previous scholarship in industrial-organizational psychology that has examined the correlates of maximum performance, which is analogous to SEB skills as behavioral capacities <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Beus & Whitman, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Klehe & Anderson, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Marcus et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Sackett et al., 1988)</ref>.

text.text: However, work on maximum performance has often relied on specific, resource-intensive, task-based performance assessments, whereas the present findings show that efficient, broadband skill inventories such as the BESSI can be used to reliably and validly assess capacities across multiple domains of social, emotional, and behavioral functioning.
Incorporating SEB skill assessments to evaluate functional capacities could thus provide researchers and practitioners with a more comprehensive evaluation of individuals' potential in the workplace.
A related implication pertains to career coaching and vocational guidance.

The present findings suggest that individuals with different SEB skill profiles gravitate toward different occupations, derive meaning and value from different kinds of workplace rewards, and succeed in different ways.
For example, individuals with highly developed Innovation Skills may be drawn to investigative and artistic careers, placing special value on the autonomy and variety afforded by this work.

In contrast, workers with strong Social Engagement Skills may show a preference for enterprising roles, highly value occupational prestige, and consistently achieve higher levels of managerial attainment and earnings.

Asset-focused career coaches, as well as vocational training and professional development programs, could draw on these insights to guide individuals into career paths that align with their key strengths.
Doing so would help promote job fit, increase job satisfaction, decrease voluntary turnover, and promote objective career attainment (Barrick et al., 2003; Cable & Edwards, 2004).
text.formatted: Doing so would help promote job fit, increase job satisfaction, decrease voluntary turnover, and promote objective career attainment <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barrick et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cable & Edwards, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: A focus on functional capacities could also help inform workplace training and development programs (Day et al., 2014).
text.formatted: A focus on functional capacities could also help inform workplace training and development programs <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Day et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas personality traits are generally conceptualized as stable dispositions, SEB skills represent learned capacities that can be developed and refined over time.
Such skill development can accumulate naturally over time, and can be further catalyzed by interventions that incorporate deliberate practice and targeted feedback (Soto et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Such skill development can accumulate naturally over time, and can be further catalyzed by interventions that incorporate deliberate practice and targeted feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Soto et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The skill-outcome links identified by the present findings can thus provide an evidence-based roadmap for employee development (Lacerenza et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The skill-outcome links identified by the present findings can thus provide an evidence-based roadmap for employee development <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Lacerenza et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For example, to help promote organizational citizenship and positive social relationships, an organization could design a training program aimed at developing Social Engagement and Cooperation Skills in newly formed project teams (Tannenbaum & Salas, 2020).

text.text: The program might involve guided exercises that require employees to practice clear communication, active listening, and group decision-making in simulated work scenarios, followed by targeted feedback from teammates and facilitators.
As another example, a program targeting Emotional Resilience Skills could help reduce burnout in frontline customer service representatives.

These employees might participate in role-playing scenarios with real-time coaching feedback to help develop their capacity to regulate stress, manage anger, and maintain composure during challenging interactions.
By focusing on the development of particular SEB skills, organizational training initiatives could help employees build the functional capacities needed for success in their roles.
A final noteworthy implication concerns the efficient assessment of SEB skills in applied workplace settings.

Organizations often need to minimize survey administration time to manage organizational costs and prevent respondent fatigue, thereby maintaining high completion rates and data quality (Stanton et al., 2002).

text.text: Thus, organizational researchers and practitioners can use these brief measures to efficiently evaluate a broad range of social, emotional, and behavioral capacities without imposing undue time burdens on respondents or excessively sacrificing validity (Credé et al., 2012; Soto & John, 2019).

text.text: The BESSI short forms could be readily integrated into large-scale screening processes, talent audits, or employee surveys.

The present research has several notable strengths, such as recruiting a large and demographically representative sample of working adults, using a multidimensional framework to assess five major domains of SEB skills, and examining an extensive array of consequential work variables.
Thus, the present findings provide a robust map of how social, emotional, and behavioral skill domains are linked with key work criteria and outcomes.
However, these findings should also be interpreted with some important limitations in mind.
For example, the present research employed a cross-sectional design.
Because all data were collected at a single point in time, we cannot establish temporal precedence or causal relations of SEB skills with work criteria and outcomes.
Intuitively, it seems likely that deploying key functional capacities in the workplace can lead to high job performance, positive work attitudes, and other outcomes.

However, reciprocal processes are also plausible, such that occupying a challenging, prestigious, or deeply rewarding role at work could shape an employee's capabilities and self-perceptions over time (Denissen et al., 2014; Wille & De Fruyt, 2014).
text.formatted: However, reciprocal processes are also plausible, such that occupying a challenging, prestigious, or deeply rewarding role at work could shape an employee's capabilities and self-perceptions over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Denissen et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Wille & De Fruyt, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, longitudinal research that tracks SEB skills and work outcomes is an important next step to map developmental trajectories, and to distinguish between directional selection and socialization effects.
A second important limitation is the reliance on self-report measures of SEB skills and many work criteria and outcomes.
This introduces the risk of common method variance, which could artificially inflate observed skill-outcome associations (Avolio et al., 1992; Spector, 1994).
text.formatted: This introduces the risk of common method variance, which could artificially inflate observed skill-outcome associations <ref type="bibr">(Avolio et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Spector, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, measuring SEB skills through self-evaluations captures how well individuals believe they can perform specific kinds of behaviors, rather than directly observing their competence levels.

The present research partially mitigated concerns about common method bias by analyzing some more-objective indicators of occupational success (such as earnings, managerial level, and attainment coded from job descriptions), and by focusing on findings that remained robust across regression analyses controlling for overlap among the skill domains.
However, future research is still needed to replicate and extend the present findings using alternative data sources (Connelly & Ones, 2010; Oh et al., 2011).
text.formatted: However, future research is still needed to replicate and extend the present findings using alternative data sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Connelly & Ones, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Oh et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: For example, incorporating supervisor or peer ratings of SEB skills, job performance, and workplace behaviors, alongside objective human resources data like actual turnover or verified salary, would provide a stronger test of skilloutcome links.

A third limitation is that although our findings show that SEB skills relate with many consequential work criteria and outcomes that have been previously linked to personality traits, they should not be interpreted as indicating whether SEB skills or personality traits provide incremental validity over each other.

Based on previous findings in predominantly student populations, we would expect that SEB skills and personality traits often show similar relations with work criteria and outcomes, but can also show unique associations and incremental validity (Chen et al., 2024; Ringwald et al., 2025; Soto et al., 2022 Soto et al., , 2023 Soto et al., , 2024;; Yoon et al., 2024).

text.text: However, additional research that assesses both SEB skills and personality traits is needed to directly test this hypothesis in the workplace context.
A final limitation concerns the composition and cultural context of the present sample.

Although our quota sampling approach successfully yielded a demographically representative cohort of full-time working adults in the United States, the present findings may not fully generalize to other populations or cultural contexts.
For example, skill-outcome associations may differ among workers who hold part-time jobs.

Moreover, cultural norms could influence the development of some SEB skills, as well as the implications of these skills for individuals' career paths and eventual workplace success (He et al. 2019; Salgado, 1997).
text.formatted: Moreover, cultural norms could influence the development of some SEB skills, as well as the implications of these skills for individuals' career paths and eventual workplace success <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(He et al. 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Salgado, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, future research is needed to test whether the implications of SEB skills for work criteria and outcomes generalize across other populations and cultural contexts.
In sum, the present research demonstrates that social, emotional, and behavioral skills are robustly linked with consequential work criteria and outcomes.
By conceptualizing and operationalizing these characteristics as functional capacities, researchers and practitioners can advance the understanding and prediction of workplace success.

The present findings indicate that assessing an individual's capacities to manage goals and tasks, engage socially, cooperate with others, regulate emotions, and learn from novel experiences can provide key insights into their potential for work performance, attainment, attitudes, intentions, behaviors, interests, and values.
Moreover, brief assessments of SEB skills can efficiently measure these capacities without imposing undue burdens on respondents or organizations.
Thus, putting social, emotional, and behavioral skills to work could help inform evidence-based approaches to fostering individual career success and organizational effectiveness.

text.text: SEB skill domains relate with a comprehensive set of consequential work criteria and outcomes.

Moreover, because organizational research and practice often dictates time-restricted assessments, it is important to establish whether links of SEB skills with criteria and work outcomes are retained when using brief measures.
To address these needs, the primary goal of the present research was to test links of SEB skills with consequential work criteria and outcomes.

Specifically, we examined how Self-Management, Social Engagement, Cooperation, Emotional Resilience, and Innovation Skills relate with key indicators of (a) occupational attainment and self-perceived performance, (b) work attitudes, (c) work behaviors and intentions, (d) vocational interests, and (e) work values in a demographically representative sample of full-time working adults.

The three UWES-3 items ("At my work, I feel bursting with energy," "I am enthusiastic about my job," "I am immersed in my work") are statements that participants rated on a seven-point frequency scale ranging from1 = never to7 = always.
In the present sample, omega reliabilities were .93 for job satisfaction, .82 for organizational commitment, .89 for work engagement, and .81 for burnout.

Taken together, these findings indicate that SEB skills relate robustly with a broad range of consequential work criteria and outcomes, and that different skill domains show distinctive relationships with different criteria and outcomes.

Most notably, (a) Social Engagement Skills relate consistently with occupational attainment, (b) Self-Management Skills with self-perceived performance, (c) Emotional Resilience Skills with work attitudes, and (d) people with different skills are interested in different kinds of jobs and value different aspects of their work.
